questions.q: The integrating factor of the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = x^4 - 3x$ is :
questions.solution:
First put the equation into standard linear form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ by dividing through by $x$ :

$$ rac{dy}{dx} -  rac{1}{x}y = x^3 - 3.$$

So $P = -\dfrac{1}{x}$.

The integrating factor is

$$	ext{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{\int - rac{1}{x}dx} = e^{-\log x} = e^{\log x^{-1}} = x^{-1}.$$

The step that is easy to skip is the division by $x$ — reading $P$ off the equation before it is in standard form gives the wrong answer.

questions.q: The integrating factor of the differential equation $\left(1 - x^2\right)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = ax$, $-1 < x < 1$, is :
questions.solution:
Divide through by $\left(1 - x^2ight)$ to reach standard form :

$$ rac{dy}{dx} +  rac{x}{1 - x^2}\,y =  rac{ax}{1 - x^2}, \qquad P =  rac{x}{1 - x^2}.$$

Now integrate $P$. Put $u = 1 - x^2$, so $du = -2x\,dx$ and $x\,dx = -	frac12 du$ :

$$\int  rac{x}{1 - x^2}dx = - rac12\int rac{du}{u} = - rac12\log u = - rac12\log\left(1 - x^2ight).$$

(The condition $-1 < x < 1$ is what makes $1 - x^2$ positive, so the logarithm is defined.)

Therefore

$$	ext{I.F.} = e^{- rac12\log(1 - x^2)} = \left(1 - x^2ight)^{-1/2} =  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}.$$

questions.q: The integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y\tan x = 2x + x^2\tan x$ is :
questions.solution:
The equation is already in standard linear form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, with

$$P = 	an x.$$

So

$$	ext{I.F.} = e^{\int 	an x\,dx} = e^{\log|\sec x|} = \sec x.$$

(Recall $\int 	an x\,dx = \log|\sec x| + c$.)

As a check, multiplying the equation by $\sec x$ gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\sec xight) = \left(2x + x^2	an xight)\sec x$, and the right-hand side is exactly $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2 \sec xight)$ — so the solution is $y\sec x = x^2\sec x + c$, i.e. $y = x^2 + c\cos x$.

questions.q: The general solution of a differential equation of order $n$ contains:
questions.solution:
Each integration introduces one constant, and reaching the solution of an $n$th-order equation takes $n$ of them.

So the general solution carries $\mathbf{n}$ arbitrary constants — and it takes $n$ extra pieces of information (initial conditions) to pin down a particular solution.

questions.q: Which of these is a variable-separable differential equation?
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = xy$ tears apart cleanly: $\dfrac{dy}{y} = x\,dx$, one variable on each side.

The others mix $x$ and $y$ in a sum, which no rearrangement separates — those need the linear or homogeneous method instead.

questions.q: Find the degree of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{4} = x$.
questions.solution:
The highest derivative is $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$, and it appears to the power $\mathbf{2}$.

The fourth power on the first derivative does not matter — degree looks only at the highest-order derivative.

questions.q: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x$ given that $y = 3$ when $x = 0$, and find the value of $y$ when $x = 1$.
questions.solution:
Integrating: $y = x^{2} + C$.

The condition $y(0) = 3$ gives $C = 3$, so $y = x^{2} + 3$.

At $x = 1$: $y = \mathbf{4}$.

The condition is what picks one curve out of the whole family.

questions.q: For $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2y}{x} = x$, the integrating factor is a function of $x$. Find its value at $x = 3$.
questions.solution:
$P = \dfrac{2}{x}$, so the factor is $e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx} = e^{2\log x} = x^{2}$.

At $x = 3$: $\mathbf{9}$.

$e^{\log(\text{something})}$ collapsing back to that something is the step worth watching for — it is what keeps integrating factors from looking frightening.

questions.q: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y$ with $y = 2$ when $x = 0$, and find $y$ when $x = \log 2$.
questions.solution:
Separating: $\dfrac{dy}{y} = dx \Rightarrow \log|y| = x + c \Rightarrow y = Ae^{x}$.

$y(0) = 2$ gives $A = 2$, so $y = 2e^{x}$.

At $x = \log 2$: $y = 2e^{\log 2} = 2 \times 2 = \mathbf{4}$.

'Rate of change equals current size' is the equation of every compound-interest account and every growing culture of bacteria.

questions.q: Find the order of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\right)^{2} + \sin\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0$.
questions.solution:
The highest derivative appearing is $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}$, so the order is $\mathbf{3}$.

Its **degree** is undefined, by the way: $\sin\left(\tfrac{dy}{dx}\right)$ stops the equation ever being a polynomial in the derivatives.

Separate the variables — each side gets only its own letter:

$\dfrac{dy}{1 + y^{2}} = \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^{2}}$.

Integrate both sides:

$\tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}x + C$.

$\mathbf{y = \tan\left(\tan^{-1}x + C\right)}$, or equivalently $\tan^{-1}y - \tan^{-1}x = C$.

Leaving the answer in the inverse-tangent form is perfectly acceptable, and usually tidier.

It is linear with $P = 2$ and $Q = e^{3x}$, so the integrating factor is $e^{\int 2dx} = e^{2x}$.

Multiply through:

$e^{2x}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2e^{2x}y = e^{5x} \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right) = e^{5x}$.

Integrate both sides:

$ye^{2x} = \dfrac{e^{5x}}{5} + C$.

$\mathbf{y = \dfrac{e^{3x}}{5} + Ce^{-2x}}$.

The integrating factor's only job is to make the left-hand side collapse into a single derivative — after that it is ordinary integration.

Every term has the same total degree, so put $y = vx$, giving $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

The right-hand side becomes $\dfrac{x + vx}{x} = 1 + v$.

So $v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = 1 + v \Rightarrow x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = 1$.

$dv = \dfrac{dx}{x} \Rightarrow v = \log|x| + C$.

Substituting back $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$:

$\mathbf{y = x\left(\log|x| + C\right)}$.

**Check:** differentiating gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \log|x| + C + 1 = \dfrac{y}{x} + 1 = \dfrac{x+y}{x}$. ✓

The substitution $y = vx$ measures $y$ in units of $x$; in those units the equation forgets its scale and separates.

questions.q: Form the differential equation of the family of circles $x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$, where $a$ is arbitrary.
questions.solution:
There is **one** arbitrary constant, so the differential equation will be of order one — differentiate once and eliminate $a$.

$2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$.

$a$ has already vanished, because it only ever appeared as a constant:

$\mathbf{x + y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0}$.

Read it geometrically: the slope at any point is $-\tfrac{x}{y}$, which says the tangent is perpendicular to the radius — true of every circle centred at the origin, whatever its size. That is exactly what removing $a$ means.

questions.q: Find the particular solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}$ given that $y = 2$ when $x = 1$.
questions.solution:
Separate: $\dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{dx}{x}$.

Integrate: $\log|y| = \log|x| + c \Rightarrow y = Ax$.

Apply $y(1) = 2$: $A = 2$.

$\mathbf{y = 2x}$ — one straight line out of the whole family of lines through the origin.
